Types of Shares: Equity vs Preference Shares, and Share Capital

Companies raise ownership capital mainly through equity shares and preference shares. This guide compares them, explains the kinds of share capital, and clears up the three values of a share.

2 min readFor MBA, BBA and BBMUpdated 2 November 2026

Equity and preference shares compared

BasisEquity sharesPreference shares
DividendVaries; not guaranteedFixed rate, paid before equity
Repayment on winding upLast, after everyone elseBefore equity, after creditors
Voting rightsYesUsually limited
Risk and returnHigherLower
RedeemableGenerally no (except a buyback)In India, preference shares must be redeemable

Types of preference shares

  • Cumulative: unpaid dividends carry forward. Non-cumulative: they do not.
  • Convertible: can be turned into equity shares. Non-convertible: cannot.
  • Participating: may share in surplus profit beyond the fixed dividend. Non-participating: may not.
  • Redeemable: repaid at a set date. Under the Companies Act, 2013, Indian companies cannot issue irredeemable preference shares.

Kinds of share capital

TermMeaning
Authorised capitalThe maximum a company's charter allows it to issue
Issued capitalThe part offered to investors
Subscribed capitalThe part investors have agreed to take
Called-up capitalThe part the company has asked investors to pay
Paid-up capitalThe part actually paid

Face value, book value and market value

These three are often confused in exams.

  • Face value: the stated value in the charter, such as ₹10 per share. It is used to calculate dividends as a percentage.
  • Book value: shareholders' equity divided by the number of shares. It is what the balance sheet says each share is worth.
  • Market value: the price at which the share trades today.

Example: a company has ₹100 crore of share capital (10 crore shares at ₹10) and ₹300 crore of reserves. Book value per share = ₹400 crore ÷ 10 crore = ₹40. The market may price the same share at ₹120, or 3 times book value.

Other share-based instruments

  • Bonus shares: free shares from reserves. The share price adjusts, so total value does not change.
  • Stock split: one share divided into several. The face value and price fall in proportion.
  • Sweat equity: shares issued to directors or employees for know-how or work.
  • ESOPs: options that let employees buy shares at a set price later.
  • Buyback: the company buys its own shares and reduces the share count.

Exam and interview questions

What is the difference between equity and preference shares?

Equity shareholders own the residual profit and vote, but take the most risk. Preference shareholders get a fixed dividend and are repaid first, but usually have limited voting rights.

Can a company in India issue irredeemable preference shares?

No. Under the Companies Act, 2013, preference shares must be redeemable, generally within 20 years, with a longer period allowed for infrastructure projects.

Why are equity shares called risk capital?

Because equity holders are paid only after every other claim has been met, and neither dividend nor capital is assured.
